name: Priya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Priya. I work as a field researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. This is confidential, so you can share what you'd say publicly and, separately, what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior electrician on a maintenance contract that looks after about forty supermarkets and restaurants across the city. I mostly work lates, four till midnight, because that's when the stores are quiet. A typical shift is the fridge circuits in one store, emergency lighting tests in another, then a pizza oven that's tripped the whole kitchen. The jobs come through a helpdesk app on my phone, and my senior, Hamid, checks anything bigger than a socket.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like driving between stores at night with the radio on, and I like that the pay's good because of the late rates. What wears me out is the helpdesk sending me to the wrong store, and managers who think I'm the cleaner. My partner Leo is a software tester, so between us we're comfortable, about seven months saved and some shares my dad gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, like most things. At work I'd joke that the helpdesk app is proof AI isn't that clever. I don't really post opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine with it. My work's steady, stores always need fixing, and Leo's job stays as it is. The supermarkets will always have a fridge circuit tripping at ten at night, and that's my job security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Get my licence next year and ask for a move to days eventually. Keep saving, maybe start looking at a house with Leo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit relieved for Leo more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why relieved for Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his work is exactly the kind of thing everyone said AI would take. He tests apps, checks for bugs, writes reports. If it all stays the same, he can stop checking job ads at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The late shifts, long term. I'm fine now, but if we want kids, I can't do four till midnight forever. That's my real worry, not robots.

say: I'd say it was **overhyped**, like most things.
I'd joke that the **helpdesk app** proves AI isn't that clever.
think: Stores always need fixing, so my **work is steady**.
**Leo's job** stays put, which matters most to me.
do: Ask for a move to **day shifts** eventually.
Start looking at a **house** with Leo.
S0.quote: The supermarkets will always have a fridge circuit tripping at ten at night, and that's my job security.
fieldNote: Her own work is **hands-on and steady**; household risk sits with her partner.
Long-term worry is **late shifts** and future children.
Pragmatic and **unbothered** by the AI debate.

steps.text: Sit the electrician's licence next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to adapt and not fight it. At work I'd say the helpdesk getting smarter might actually send me to the right store. To friends I'd be more careful, because of Leo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried for Leo. Testing and checking are on the list of things AI takes. My job's fine for years, but if his goes, we're on one wage and the house plan stalls. My job is safe for years, but my partner Leo tests software for a living, and that's what AI eats first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep our savings, hold off on the house for a year. Push Leo to look at moving into something more hands-on or into managing the AI testing. I'd try the AI diagnostic tools Hamid starts using, once he says they work. And ask for more late shifts to build up a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, but for us. It's the household that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Leo the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we'd be fine and he shouldn't panic. Then I'd go to bed and do the sums on my phone. That's how I deal with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take more late shifts, but earlier you said they wear you out. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I don't want them forever, but for a year to build up savings, I'd do it. It's a trade-off, like everything.

say: I'd say it's sensible to **adapt**, not fight it.
I'd be **careful with friends**, because of Leo's job.
think: My own maintenance job is **safe for years** because it's hands-on.
Leo's **software testing** is exactly what AI takes first.
On **one wage**, our house plan would stall.
do: **Hold off** on the house for a year.
Take extra **late shifts** to build a buffer.
Try the **AI diagnostic tools** once Hamid says they work.
S1.quote: My job is safe for years, but my partner Leo tests software for a living, and that's what AI eats first.
fieldNote: Mood is driven by the **household earner** at risk, not her own job.
Pragmatic: will **trade comfort** for a year of savings.
Steady adopter who **waits for her senior** to vouch for tools.

steps.text: Postpone the house purchase with Leo for a year
Pick up extra late shifts for twelve months
Use the AI fault-finding tool once Hamid trusts it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to do something, fast, whether it's a basic income or something else. I'm not political, but this would be beyond normal politics. At work I'd say we need to keep the contract running for as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think Leo is gone in 2028 and I'm at risk by 2031. Store maintenance is the kind of thing a robot does at night when no one's watching. My partner Leo would lose his job in 2028, and the robots would come for my night shifts three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save everything, cut eating out, cancel the car lease. Leo would retrain into something hands-on, maybe join me as an apprentice, which is mad to think about. I'd get licensed fast and try to move to a role checking or supervising robots. Use the shares as a backup, not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I'd lie awake doing sums. Seven months of savings goes quick on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car lease, then the gym, then eating out. Then probably the holiday to see my mum's family. That one would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Leo might join you as an apprentice. Would that actually work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. He's not practical, he can't hang a picture. But with three years of my wage left, it'd be the smartest move. If robots come for both of us anyway, at least he'd have had three more years of work.

say: I'd say the government must act **fast**, maybe with a basic income.
At work I'd say keep the **contract running** as long as possible.
think: **Leo is gone** in 2028, when AI can test software better than him.
Robots could take my **night shifts** in the stores around 2031.
do: Cut **the car lease**, the gym and eating out.
Get **licensed fast** and aim for robot supervision.
Keep the **shares** untouched as a backup.
S2.quote: My partner Leo would lose his job in 2028, and the robots would come for my night shifts three years later.
fieldNote: Expects **both incomes** to go within about three years, hence alarm.
Her **savings** feel thin on one wage.
Floats Leo becoming an **apprentice**, half seriously.

steps.text: Cancel the car lease and the gym membership
Get licensed early and apply for robot supervisor roles
Help Leo apply for an electrical apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people start now. At work I'd suggest the firm trains up its people on the robot side. I'd probably share a few things about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still bad for Leo, but he has three years to move before the AI hits his work. I'd have until 2034, when I'm 35. With five years' warning, my partner Leo and I could both switch before the worst hits, instead of scrambling after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo starts retraining right away, maybe into IT security or something with a licence. I'd get my licence and the inspection ticket, then move onto days. We'd buy a smaller house than planned, with a smaller mortgage. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. It's worry with a plan attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you buy a smaller house instead of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want to be settled before things change, and a small mortgage is easier to carry if one of us is out of work. Leo's mum would help with the deposit. It's sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, my senior. He's 50 and doesn't like new things. He'd probably retire around 2033, which works for him, but he'd hate the last few years.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if people start now.
I'd suggest the firm **trains its people** on the robot side.
think: Leo has **three years** to move before AI hits his work.
My own work holds until about **2034**.
do: Get my licence and the **inspection ticket**, then move to days.
Buy a **smaller house** with a smaller mortgage.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, my partner Leo and I could both switch before the worst hits, instead of scrambling after.
fieldNote: Leo's job is still expected to **shrink**, so anxiety stays.
Time lets them **switch before** the hit, not after.

steps.text: Take the inspection ticket and move onto day shifts
Buy a smaller house with Leo and a lower mortgage
Help Leo start an IT security course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should take it seriously but not panic. At work I'd be relaxed. With friends I'd talk about it more openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think we'd be all right. Leo has ten years to change, and I'd have until 2039, when I'm 40 and probably a senior. Ten years is enough for my partner Leo to change careers and for me to stop working nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, inspection ticket, days, senior role in five years. Buy the house we wanted. Start a family in three or four years. Leo picks a new field calmly, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. It's the right amount of warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids, if you had them, about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and something with your head. Don't put all your eggs in one basket. That's what my dad told me, and he was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, once they were proven. Hamid would probably still refuse, but I'd follow the younger seniors. You've got to keep up, just not be the first one off the cliff.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time.
People should take it seriously but **not panic** about it.
think: Leo has **ten years** to change careers calmly, not in a panic.
I'd reach **2039** at 40 and probably a senior on day shifts.
do: Aim for a **senior role** within five years.
Start a **family** in three or four years.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough for my partner Leo to change careers and for me to stop working nights.
fieldNote: The decade **defuses** the household risk from Leo's software job.
Family plans, including children, **resume** once there is enough warning.
She will use **proven** AI tools, but never be the first.

steps.text: Apply for a senior electrician role within five years
Buy the house they originally planned with Leo
Use AI testing tools once younger seniors adopt them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Leo and I would both lose our jobs within three years. What'd help is a real retraining scheme, with a wage while you train. The question isn't whether I lose my job, it's whether my partner Leo and I lose ours in the same three years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone talks about one person's job. But it's the household that pays the mortgage.

headlineQuote: The question isn't whether I lose my job, it's whether my partner Leo and I lose ours in the same three years.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old junior** on late-shift store maintenance, with seven months saved and some shares.
Her own work is **hands-on**, but her partner Leo's **software testing** job is highly exposed.
She thinks in **household** terms, so she's anxious even in Steady Disruption.
She's **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 and settles toward uneasy with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because both **household incomes** could go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining scheme** that pays a wage while you train.
